examTakeaway: NMDA receptors need both glutamate and a relieved magnesium block, which is why they open during strong depolarization.
scenario: A 22-year-old student is taught that a hippocampal neuron fires only when two inputs arrive together. At rest, magnesium sits in a channel. When the membrane is depolarized and glutamate is present, calcium enters. She asks which receptor let the calcium in.
question: Which receptor let the calcium in?
explanation: NMDA receptors need both glutamate and a relieved magnesium block, which is why they open during strong depolarization. NMDA is the coincidence receptor that passed calcium. AMPA alone, with no coincidence, passes sodium when glutamate binds but is not the magnesium-blocked calcium path described. GABA-A and the glycine inhibitory receptor hyperpolarize. Nicotinic muscle receptor is at the neuromuscular junction.

examTakeaway: Myelin forces saltatory conduction, so a demyelinated segment slows the impulse and may block it when hot.
scenario: A 28-year-old woman has blurred vision that worsens in a hot shower. Conduction in the affected nerve is slow, and the impulse sometimes dies in the middle of the nerve. MRI shows a white-matter plaque. She asks why heat made the impulse fail.
question: Why did heat block the impulse?
options: A demyelinated membrane cannot sustain the current when channels close faster
The synapse ran out of acetylcholine
The node of Ranvier disappeared in a healthy nerve
correctAnswer: A demyelinated membrane cannot sustain the current when channels close faster
explanation: Myelin forces saltatory conduction, so a demyelinated segment slows the impulse and may block it when hot. A demyelinated membrane cannot sustain the current when channels close faster in the heat. The synapse ran out of acetylcholine is a neuromuscular story, not a central plaque. The node of Ranvier disappeared in a healthy nerve would speed nothing; myelin loss exposes membrane between nodes. GABA increased would inhibit, not explain temperature-sensitive conduction block. The blood-brain barrier sealed is not the conduction failure.

examTakeaway: Cutting an axon causes Wallerian degeneration distal to the cut and chromatolysis in the cell body.
scenario: A 30-year-old man severs the left ulnar nerve at the elbow. A week later the nerve segment in the hand is breaking down, and the cell body in the spinal cord has a nucleus pushed aside. He asks which segment degenerates even though the cell body is still alive.
question: Which part of the neuron degenerates first distal to the cut?
options: The axon stump beyond the cut
The myelin of an untouched nerve
The neuromuscular junction of a different limb
correctAnswer: The axon stump beyond the cut
explanation: Cutting an axon causes Wallerian degeneration distal to the cut and chromatolysis in the cell body. The axon stump beyond the cut loses its supply and degenerates. The cell body only shows chromatolysis but does not die first. The contralateral cortex is not cut. The myelin of an untouched nerve stays. The neuromuscular junction of a different limb is not downstream of this ulnar cut.

examTakeaway: A lesion of the right optic tract causes a left homonymous hemianopia, because that tract has already passed the chiasm.
scenario: A 60-year-old man has a stroke. He cannot see the left half of the world with either eye. The pupils still react. The chiasm is intact on imaging. The lesion is behind the chiasm on the right. He asks why both eyes lost the same half of the field.
question: Why did both eyes lose the left field?
options: The occipital pole macula alone was lost
The right tract already carries left-field fibers from both eyes
The chiasm crossing fibers were cut
correctAnswer: The right tract already carries left-field fibers from both eyes
explanation: A lesion of the right optic tract causes a left homonymous hemianopia, because that tract has already passed the chiasm. The right tract already carries left-field fibers from both eyes, so both eyes lose the left field. The chiasm crossing fibers were cut would cause a bitemporal loss, and imaging shows the chiasm is intact. One optic nerve was cut would blind one eye. The left tract was cut would lose the right field. The occipital pole macula alone was lost would spare or hit central vision, not a clean half-field.

examTakeaway: The stretch reflex is monosynaptic, so tapping a tendon jerks the muscle with no interneuron.
scenario: A 25-year-old man's patellar tap produces a kick before he can think. The sensory neuron from the muscle spindle synapses directly on the motor neuron. There is no interneuron in that arc. He asks why this jerk is faster than a withdrawal from pain.
question: Why is the tendon jerk faster than withdrawal?
options: It uses a Golgi tendon organ as the sensor
explanation: The stretch reflex is monosynaptic, so tapping a tendon jerks the muscle with no interneuron. It is one synapse, which is why it beats a withdrawal. It uses a pain interneuron describes withdrawal, which is polysynaptic. It crosses the cord is a contralateral withdrawal path. It waits for the cortex would be a voluntary kick. It uses a Golgi tendon organ as the sensor is the inverse myotatic reflex, which inhibits the muscle.

examTakeaway: REM sleep has an active EEG and paralyzed skeletal muscle, which is why dreams are not acted out unless that paralysis fails.
scenario: A 70-year-old man thrashes and shouts during vivid dreams, and he sometimes injures his partner. Between episodes muscle tone in sleep is not suppressed the way it should be. Breathing is intact. He asks which normal sleep state failed to paralyze him.
question: Which sleep state normally paralyzes the limbs?
explanation: REM sleep has an active EEG and paralyzed skeletal muscle, which is why dreams are not acted out unless that paralysis fails. REM is the state whose atonia failed, so he acts the dream. Stage 3 slow wave is deep sleep with high-amplitude slow waves and little dreaming. Wakefulness is not the dream state. Stage 1 doze is light sleep. A coma pattern is not organized dream sleep.

examTakeaway: Referred pain from the diaphragm is felt at the shoulder because both share C3 to C5.
scenario: A 40-year-old woman has shoulder-tip pain after a laparoscopy that left free air under the diaphragm. The shoulder joint is normal. There is no arm weakness. She asks why the diaphragm's irritation is felt at the shoulder.
question: Why is diaphragmatic irritation felt at the shoulder?
options: The phrenic nerve is a lumbar root
The accessory nerve shares the diaphragm
Both are served by C3 to C5
The vagus refers pain to the hand
correctAnswer: Both are served by C3 to C5
explanation: Referred pain from the diaphragm is felt at the shoulder because both share C3 to C5. Both are served by C3 to C5, the phrenic roots and the shoulder skin. The vagus refers pain to the hand is not this map. The phrenic nerve is a lumbar root is anatomically wrong. The accessory nerve shares the diaphragm is cranial nerve XI, which does not innervate the diaphragm. Dermatomes T10 explain the shoulder is the umbilical dermatome, not the shoulder.

examTakeaway: Dopamine from the ventral tegmentum drives reward, which is why drugs that raise dopamine there are reinforcing.
scenario: A 22-year-old man uses cocaine and describes a rush. Imaging research in similar users shows increased dopamine signaling in the nucleus accumbens. He does not have a resting tremor. He asks which midbrain cells supplied that dopamine.
question: Which cells supplied the reward dopamine?
explanation: Dopamine from the ventral tegmentum drives reward, which is why drugs that raise dopamine there are reinforcing. Ventral tegmental neurons project to the nucleus accumbens. Substantia nigra neurons that died would cause a resting tremor he does not have; that pathway is movement. Raphe serotonin neurons and locus ceruleus neurons use different transmitters. Basal nucleus cholinergic neurons are the memory projection lost in Alzheimer disease.

examTakeaway: The blood-brain barrier is tight endothelium, so a drug must be lipid soluble or use a transporter to enter the brain.
scenario: A 50-year-old man with meningitis receives a polar antibiotic that reaches high blood levels but almost no level in spinal fluid while the barrier is intact. After inflammation, the level in the fluid rises. He asks what normally keeps the polar drug out.
question: What normally keeps a polar drug out of the brain?
explanation: The blood-brain barrier is tight endothelium, so a drug must be lipid soluble or use a transporter to enter the brain. Tight endothelial junctions are the barrier, loosened by inflammation. A gap-junction choroid is not the capillary barrier. Fenestrated capillaries like the kidney would let the drug through. An absent basement membrane would not create a barrier. Free diffusion of all antibiotics is what fails here.

examTakeaway: Serotonin from the raphe helps start sleep, which is why a drug that raises serotonin can cause drowsiness.
scenario: A 40-year-old woman starts an SSRI and is sleepy for the first week. She has no tremor and no muscle rigidity. The prescriber says a brainstem nucleus that uses serotonin is being pushed harder. She asks which nucleus.
question: Which nucleus is being pushed?
options: The locus ceruleus as a pure serotonin source
explanation: Serotonin from the raphe helps start sleep, which is why a drug that raises serotonin can cause drowsiness. The raphe is the serotonin nucleus. The substantia nigra and the ventral tegmental area use dopamine. The nucleus basalis uses acetylcholine. The locus ceruleus as a pure serotonin source is wrong; that nucleus uses norepinephrine.

examTakeaway: Norepinephrine from the locus ceruleus supports alertness, so drugs that raise it can cause insomnia.
scenario: A 35-year-old man starts bupropion and cannot fall asleep. He has no galactorrhea. The drug raises norepinephrine and dopamine and does not raise serotonin much. He asks which brainstem nucleus, if overdriven, keeps him awake.
question: Which nucleus, overdriven, keeps him awake?
options: The raphe as the main norepinephrine source
explanation: Norepinephrine from the locus ceruleus supports alertness, so drugs that raise it can cause insomnia. The locus ceruleus is that norepinephrine nucleus. The raphe as the main norepinephrine source is the serotonin nucleus instead. The supraoptic nucleus releases ADH. The Edinger-Westphal nucleus constricts the pupil. The nucleus ambiguus is a vagal motor nucleus.

examTakeaway: Golgi tendon organs fire when tension is high and inhibit the same muscle, protecting it from overload.
scenario: A 20-year-old weightlifter drops a bar when the load suddenly feels too heavy, before the muscle tears. The sensor was in the tendon, not the muscle belly. The motor neuron to that muscle was inhibited. He asks what the tendon sensor did.
question: What did the tendon sensor do?
options: Contracted the antagonist only by a stretch reflex
Fired because the muscle was slack
explanation: Golgi tendon organs fire when tension is high and inhibit the same muscle, protecting it from overload. Inhibited the same muscle is the inverse myotatic reflex. Excited the same muscle is the spindle stretch reflex. Contracted the antagonist only by a stretch reflex is not the tendon organ's main protective act. Caused clonus is an upper-motor oscillation. Fired because the muscle was slack is the opposite; the organ fires when tension is high.
